previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: Mr. ___ was admitted due to groin pain and a positive urine culture, raising concern for a urinary tract infection. However, evaluation revealed no signs of systemic infection—afebrile, normal white blood cell count, and no bacteremia. The positive culture was attributed to chronic ESBL E. coli colonization and mixed flora consistent with contamination. Physical exam identified a 3 cm tender, erythematous lesion on the glans penis, diagnosed as tinea cruris, contributing to discomfort. Pain was managed with acetaminophen, and a topical antifungal (miconazole powder) was initiated. Antibiotics were discontinued after one dose of IV Zosyn, as symptoms were deemed due to catheter irritation and fungal infection rather than active UTI. The patient was counseled on catheter hygiene, suprapubic catheter as a potential long-term option, and discharged home with follow-up planned with his PCP and urologist.
